slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real system you have access to (a CRM export, an HR roster, a customer list) and list every field in it that counts as PII: direct identifiers (name, SSN, email) separated from quasi-identifiers that could combine to re-identify someone (ZIP code plus birth date plus gender, for example).
slots.deliverable: A written PII field inventory from a real dataset, split into direct identifiers and quasi-identifiers.

lessons.title: Regulations: GDPR, CCPA and HIPAA Overview

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same dataset from the previous slot, flag any field that goes beyond plain PII into sensitive or confidential territory (health status, financial detail, trade secret), then decide which of GDPR, CCPA, or HIPAA would actually apply to that data and write one sentence on the specific obligation each imposes.
slots.deliverable: A short note flagging sensitive/confidential fields plus the applicable regulation(s) and one obligation each creates.

slots.practicalActivity: Identify one industry rule (SOX or a sector-specific rule) that would apply to an organization you know, and name one financial or operational record it governs. Then pick a system you're building or have used, and list three privacy-by-design decisions that should have been made before a single line of code was written (what to collect, how long to keep it, who defaults to seeing it).
slots.deliverable: One named regulation with the record it governs, plus three privacy-by-design decisions for a real or familiar system.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a spreadsheet or table you have access to that you didn't personally create. Without being told what's in it, scan its column names for anything that looks sensitive (names, dates of birth, identifiers, financial figures), then open a few rows to check whether the actual content matches what the column name implied. Note any mismatch -- a generic column name holding something sensitive, or a sensitive-sounding name that's actually harmless.
slots.deliverable: A written note on one real column-name-vs-content mismatch found during a manual discovery pass.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a 4-tier classification scheme (e.g., Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) and assign a tier to every field you inventoried two slots ago. Then write one governance rule for keeping that scheme current (who re-reviews a label when a column's purpose changes, and how often).
slots.deliverable: A 4-tier classification scheme applied to a real field list, plus one written governance rule for keeping labels current.

slots.practicalActivity: Classification lab: take the full field inventory built across this chapter's slots and produce one end-to-end classification worksheet -- every field, its discovery method (pattern, keyword, or sampling), its assigned tier, and the governance owner responsible for re-reviewing that label.
slots.deliverable: A complete classification worksheet covering discovery method, tier, and governance owner for every inventoried field.

slots.practicalActivity: On a test database (never production), run CREATE ROLE, GRANT SELECT on one table to that role, add yourself as a member with ALTER ROLE ... ADD MEMBER, then query sys.database_permissions to see the grant you created. Run a DENY on one column of that table and note how it changes what you can query even though the role still grants SELECT on the table overall.
slots.deliverable: A working test-database role with a GRANT, a membership addition, and a column-level DENY, with the resulting permission query output.

slots.practicalActivity: Name one real or plausible segregation-of-duties conflict in your organization (the same person who approves a payment can also create the vendor record, for example), and describe one control that would separate those duties. Then design a quarterly access-review checklist covering both ordinary roles and privileged accounts.
slots.deliverable: One described segregation-of-duties conflict with its control, plus a quarterly access-review checklist.

slots.practicalActivity: Access governance lab: using the roles created earlier in this chapter, build a permission matrix (roles down the side, tables/columns across the top, GRANT/DENY/blank in each cell) for a 3-5 table slice of a database you know, then run the matrix against the least-privilege test: for each cell, write one sentence justifying why that role needs that exact access, no more.
slots.deliverable: A role-by-table permission matrix with a one-sentence least-privilege justification for every granted cell.

slots.practicalActivity: On a test database, create a table with a fake SSN and email column, populate a few rows, then apply Dynamic Data Masking: partial() on the SSN column and email() on the email column. Query the table as the table owner (who bypasses masking) and then as a lower-privileged test user, and compare the two result sets side by side.
slots.deliverable: A masked test table with two side-by-side query result sets (privileged vs. masked view) and a note on what each function hid.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one paragraph on where the encryption key for the data you masked in the previous slot should actually live (not in the same database as the data it protects), and who should be allowed to rotate it. Then sketch a row-security rule that would restrict a sales-rep role to only their own region's rows in a real or sample Orders table.
slots.deliverable: A written key-custody note plus one sketched row-security filter rule for a real table.

slots.practicalActivity: Protecting-data lab: on the test table from the masking slot, add the UNMASK permission for one narrow role (GRANT UNMASK TO ...), confirm that role can now see real values while every other role still sees the mask, then write the row-security policy statement you'd add on top to also restrict that role to one region's rows -- combining masking, UNMASK, and row security in one working example.
slots.deliverable: A test table with masking, a scoped UNMASK grant, and a written row-security policy layered on top, with before/after query results.

lessons.title: Data Deletion and the Right to Erasure

slots.practicalActivity: Write a retention schedule for the classified fields from Chapter 2 (how long each tier is kept and why), then draft the step-by-step process you'd actually run if a customer submitted a right-to-erasure request against that same dataset -- which systems would need touching, and what would prove the deletion happened.
slots.deliverable: A retention schedule by classification tier, plus a written right-to-erasure handling process for one real dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: List the three or four events on your protected test table from earlier (a DENY change, an UNMASK grant, a deletion) that absolutely must be logged for audit, and name what each log entry needs to capture. Then outline a five-step breach-response plan for a scenario where that table's masked SSN column was found exposed in a report export.
slots.deliverable: A list of must-log events with required fields, plus a five-step breach-response outline for a concrete exposure scenario.

lessons.title: Security and Privacy Case Study: Customer Data

slots.practicalActivity: Working through the lesson's customer-data case study, apply the same reasoning to your own classification worksheet from Chapter 2: name the roles that should see each tier, the masking or encryption control each tier needs, and the retention period that applies. Then draft a one-page access governance model (roles, their access to each tier, and who approves exceptions) for that same dataset.
slots.deliverable: A tier-by-tier control mapping (roles, protection, retention) plus a one-page access governance model for a real dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short privacy impact assessment (PIA) for the dataset you've been working with across this course: what personal data it holds, why it's collected, who has access, what could go wrong, and what controls (from the Protecting Data and Access Control chapters) mitigate each risk.
slots.deliverable: A written privacy impact assessment covering data held, access, risks, and mitigating controls for one real dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: assemble everything built across this course into one security-and-privacy package for a single real dataset -- the PII/sensitive-field inventory, the classification worksheet, the RBAC permission matrix, the masking/encryption/row-security controls applied, the retention schedule, and the PIA. Present it as if handing it to an auditor who has never seen the dataset.
slots.deliverable: A consolidated security-and-privacy package (inventory, classification, access matrix, protection controls, retention, PIA) for one real dataset.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can inventory and classify sensitive data in a real dataset, design and implement a least-privilege RBAC model with real GRANT/DENY/role statements, apply masking and row/column security controls with working T-SQL, and produce a retention plan and privacy impact assessment -- the hands-on security vocabulary Microsoft Purview's governance workflows and policies build on next in this path.
